subtopicTitle: Regular languages — closed under union, intersection, complement, concatenation, Kleene star

cards.front: What does it mean that regular languages are closed under union?
cards.back: If L1 and L2 are regular then L1 ∪ L2 is regular.

cards.front: Are regular languages closed under intersection, complement, concatenation and Kleene star?
cards.back: Yes: the class is closed under all five operations (union, intersection, complement, concatenation, Kleene star).

cards.front: Describe the NFA construction realizing closure under union.
cards.back: Given NFAs M1, M2: create new start s0 with ε-edges to starts of M1 and M2; accept states = union of both accept sets.

cards.front: Give the NFA construction for concatenation of two regular languages.
cards.back: From NFAs M1, M2 add ε-edges from every accept state of M1 to the start of M2; new accept states = accept states of M2 only.

cards.front: How is closure under intersection obtained from the other closures?
cards.back: L1 ∩ L2 = complement(complement(L1) ∪ complement(L2)) via De Morgan; closure under union and complement implies closure under intersection.

cards.front: Prove regular languages are closed under complement using DFAs.
cards.back: Let M be a complete DFA for L. Swap accepting and non-accepting states to obtain a DFA for the complement language. Determinism and totality guarantee every string is accepted by exactly one of the two machines.

cards.front: State the NFA construction for the Kleene star of a regular language.
cards.back: Add new state s0 (both start and accept) with ε-edge to old start; add ε-edges from every old accept state back to old start and also an ε-loop on s0 (handles ε).

cards.front: Why does the Kleene-star NFA construction correctly accept L*?
cards.back: Any number of concatenations is realized by looping via the new ε-edges; the extra ε-loop on the new start state accepts the empty string.
